You measure concentration over time in order to obtain a rate.
A rate law expresses the rate that was just defined in terms of concentrations.
Collision theory motivates why rate depends on concentration.
Reaction order is the exponent in the rate law.
The initial-rates method uses measured concentration-time data.
The method's purpose is to determine reaction order.
The first-order integrated law applies to a first-order reaction.
The integrated law is fitted to concentration-time data.
The second-order integrated law applies to a second-order reaction.
The second-order derivation parallels the first-order one.
Half-life is derived directly from the integrated rate laws.
Half-life behaviour differs between first and second order.
Activation energy is the minimum collision energy from collision theory.
The Arrhenius equation contains the activation energy explicitly.
The Arrhenius equation describes how the rate constant of the rate law varies with temperature.
Mechanisms are proposed to explain the observed rate law.
The rate-determining step is one of the elementary steps in a mechanism.
Deriving a rate law from the slow step requires understanding order.
Catalysis works by lowering the activation energy.
A catalyst introduces an alternative mechanistic pathway.
Validating a mechanism means deriving its rate law from the slow step and comparing to data.
The experimental rate law used for validation comes from methods like initial rates.
Temperature dependence can corroborate a proposed mechanism.
